data.title: Voto Latino reveals six-figure Texas investment alongside Talarico, Hinojosa event
data.description:
Voto Latino on Friday unveiled a new six-figure investment aimed at boosting Latino voter engagement in Texas with early voting kicking off in the state next week. 

The civic engagement organization said in a news release first shared with The Hill that it was investing over $500,000 in the state. The investment comes ahead of the group’s event in the Rio Grande Valley later this month with Democratic candidates running in closely-watched midterm races. 

President Trump and Republicans seen his support among Latino voters slip heading into the November elections, in which he has repeatedly urged Americans to cast their votes as if he were “on the ballot.” This voting demographic was key to the president’s 2024 victory in the state.

Maria Teresa Kumar, the group’s president and co-founder, called Texas “ground zero for change” in a statement announcing this investment.

“We are heading straight to the epicenter of the Latino vote to make sure every voter is ready to cast their ballot,” Kumar said. “Latinos are on the brink of changing the political landscape of Texas and the nation.”

The group’s Oct. 25 event will feature three Democratic candidates in tightly-contested midterm races, including gubernatorial nominee Gina Hinojosa, Senate hopeful James Talarico and House candidate Bobby Pulido. 

Hinojosa, who is running to unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), said there was “no better place” to close out her campaign. 

“For too long, Texans have been paying more and getting less under Greg Abbott,” she said in a statement. “I’m proud to be joining Voto Latino, making sure every family in the Valley has the information and the power to make their voice heard from now until Election Day.” 

Talarico is running in a tightly-contested race against Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R).

“Latino families in Texas have always carried this state forward, and they should have leaders who listen and deliver,” he said in a statement. “Our democracy works best when every neighbor has a seat at the table, and I’m grateful to Voto Latino for bringing us together for these final days.”

Pulido, a Latin Grammy-winning singer from the Rio Grande Valley, is running in the state’s 15th District against incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz.

“What I hear from families isn’t about left or right. They want good jobs, affordable health care, and schools that give their kids a real shot,” he said in a statement. “Our community has always shown up for one another, and I’m proud to be here with Voto Latino to make sure every voice in the Valley is heard.”

data.title: Trump claims neither he nor Musk caused Ukraine Starlink outage
data.description:
President Trump claimed on Friday that neither he nor SpaceX founder Elon Musk caused Ukraine’s Starlink outage earlier this week as the president clashed with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky over resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries.

“I didn’t do that. No, we didn’t do that at all. In fact, I don’t even think it was slowed down from what I understood. Because I just checked this morning,” Trump told reporters Friday while on his way to a campaign rally in Georgia.

“I heard about it from the news, the media. And we didn’t slow it down at all. And I think it’s probably functioning, from what I understand,” he continued. 

When asked by a reporter if Musk was involved, Trump said, “I don’t know if there’s anybody because it wasn’t me, and it wasn’t Elon as I understand.”

A White House official similarly told NewsNation, a sister network of The Hill, that “no such request” was ever made by Trump.

The outage was reported by Ukraine Wednesday, saying that its military lost access to the military version of Starlink, which it uses for vital communications.

Starlink services were cut off specifically for objects that traveled more than 100 mph, impacting the capabilities of Ukraine’s drones, airplanes and helicopters, a source familiar with the matter told The Hill.

At the time, some Ukrainian officials speculated the decision to restrict its access may have come from Washington.

Musk initially deferred to Trump, saying on the social platform X, “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.”

“Starlink is a commercial service owned and controlled by SpaceX. Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company,” Musk wrote.

The conflict over access to Starlink marked a flashpoint in relations between Zelensky and Trump as he said the Ukrainian president was “not a good guy for us to deal with.”

Multiple GOP senators expressed concern earlier this week that loss of access to critical Starlink servers had “degraded Ukraine’s ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure.”

“Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation,” the group of GOP senators wrote in a letter to Platte Moring, the Pentagon’s inspector general.

data.title: Ocasio-Cortez makes $1M donation to El-Sayed Senate bid
data.description:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) made a $1 million donation to Abdul El-Sayed’s (D) Michigan Senate campaign, a campaign spokesperson confirmed to The Hill on Friday.

El-Sayed is locked in a tight contest for Michigan’s U.S. Senate seat, facing off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.). Ocasio-Cortez said she made the donation because she did not want to regret not doing more for El-Sayed if he loses.

“I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement to The Hill. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.”

Nonpartisan election forecaster Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), a partner of The Hill, gives El-Sayed a 68 percent chance of winning the Michigan Senate race.

The New York congresswoman said she made the donation using campaign funds from more than 2 million donors, not from her personal wealth.

“It is not MY contribution. It is OUR contribution,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a fundraising email.

Ocasio-Cortez is criss-crossing the nation ahead of the midterms, rallying with other progressives including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign tour for El-Sayed has included multiple stops across Michigan this week.

This cycle, Ocasio-Cortez has been more selective with her endorsements. She endorsed in only a handful of the congressional Democratic primary fights. She chose to endorse El-Sayed in his primary against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), whom he defeated narrowly. She also endorsed a slate of progressive candidates in the New York state legislative primaries.

Her endorsements and rallies have increased speculation that she may choose to run for president in 2028. While she has not yet made up her mind on the decision, she told the New York Times last month that she may only get one chance.

“Life doesn’t wait for you to be ready for things,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “Sometimes life just makes things ready for you.”

data.title: Mamdani, New York Democrats call on private parking lot owners to ban ICE agents
data.description:
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and other Empire State Democratic leaders urged the city’s private parking lot owners Friday to ban Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents from their properties. 

“In solidarity with immigrant New Yorkers and in our shared commitment to the City we love, we ask that you do not rent, lend or otherwise make your property available to ICE as a staging area for its enforcement operations,” the mayor wrote in a letter to owners and operators of these properties.

Over 100 elected officials, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), signed on to Mamdani’s request.

The New York Democrats cited the recent ICE-involved shooting of Oscar Belgal in the city’s Marble Hill neighborhood last week while his five-year-old son was in the car with him. 

Following the shooting, the mayor condemned the Oct. 8 shooting as “unconscionable” in a social media post and demanded that all ICE enforcement operations be halted in the city. 

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said Belgal was an immigrant who had a prior criminal conviction and arrests. 

The Friday letter pointed out that the federal immigration officials involved in this incident utilized a privately-owned parking lot during their operations. 

“Federal agents are turning to private parking lots, including a lot just blocks from where they shot Mr. Belgal,” Mamdani said in a Friday statement. “I am asking every garage and lot owner in this city to stop giving them that option. Do not rent your property to ICE. Do not lend it to them. Tell them they are not welcome.” 

The Democratic officials pointed to an executive order the mayor signed earlier this year barring external law enforcement agencies, like DHS, from staging operations on city property unless they have a judicial warrant or meet other “limited legal exceptions.”

“Time and again, New York City has made it through challenging moments because government, business and community leaders come together and show the world what New Yorkers can do,” the Democratic officials wrote in their Friday letter. “Owners who refuse to take part in these federal civil immigration enforcement operations advance public safety by protecting their own staff and customers, as well as fellow New Yorkers beyond their lots and garages.“

“They also tell every immigrant New Yorker that they are treasured members of this community and that our City welcomes them with open arms,” they continued. “We hope you will stand with us.”

A DHS spokesperson told The Hill Friday that barring federal agents from parking lots would not halt deportation operations in the city. 

“Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t,” the DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “Luckily, no terminated parking will stop ICE from deporting criminal illegal aliens to make New York safe again.”

data.title: Democrats rake in cash, Musk takes center stage for GOP: 5 takeaways from latest fundraising hauls
data.description:
Democrats running in competitive Senate races are raking in cash as they race to close the financial gap with Republicans, who have been buoyed in part by Elon Musk and his super PAC.

Democrat James Talarico’s campaign for Texas Senate alone raised a staggering $60 million between July, August and September, while Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) brought in $33 million and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed raked in close to $31 million in the Michigan Senate contest —dwarfing their GOP counterparts.

But Musk, the tech billionaire and former Trump adviser, has served as a bright spot for Republicans, with his super PAC effectively bankrolling Texas Senate GOP candidate Ken Paxton’s campaign.

This investment has made the fierce contest one of the most expensive Senate races in history — with more than $500 million spent or reserved in advertising in total between the two parties, according to ad-tracking firm AdImpact. The firm is also forecasting that the 2026 election could be the most expensive midterm cycle ever.

Here are five takeaways from the last quarterly filing before Election Day:

Democrats post blockbuster numbers in Senate races

It’s not just Talarico, Ossoff and El-Sayed who are outraising their Republican counterparts in key races.

Battleground Senate Democratic candidates have outraised their opponents: former Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown’s campaign raised $23 million, Maine’s Troy Jackson collected over $20 million, former Rep. Mary Peltola (Alaska) posted $14 million and former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper’s campaign raked in $12.2 million.

Meanwhile, Paxton’s campaign raised over $10 million, Michigan Republican Mike Rogers, a former House lawmaker, posted 9.7 million, Sen. Jon Husted (R) raised close to $5 million in Ohio, Maine Sen. Susan Collins (R) reported $5.2 million, Georgia’s Republican candidate Rep. Mike Collins posted $2.8 million, former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley, running against Cooper, reported $2.1 million and Sen. Dan Sullivan’s (R) campaign raised $2 million in Alaska. 

Adam Hamilton, a pastor running as a Democrat for the Kansas Senate, even raised more than Sen. Roger Marshall (R). The Democrat’s campaign brought in over $9 million while Marshall’s campaign reported just over $800,000. 

That doesn’t mean Republicans aren’t making those numbers up elsewhere — those figures don’t account for joint fundraising accounts, super PAC spending to benefit or oppose candidates, or their general financial advantage at a party level.  

Still, the higher campaign fundraising gives Democrats more bang for their buck with ad buys. Senate Democratic candidates also outraised their GOP peers last quarter.

Musk dives back into political fray to boost GOP

Musk and his super PAC, America PAC, have become key assets for Republicans this cycle as the GOP looks to keep parity with Democrats on fundraising. Musk donated $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) PAC, which is associated with Senate GOP leadership. 

The contributions, $75 million and $83 million, were each made to the super PAC. A day after SLF PAC received those contributions, they were immediately transferred to Texas PAC, which is a Senate GOP leadership-aligned group backing Paxton. 

Texas PAC’s quarterly report shows that Musk financed the group entirely. 

America PAC has also been very active this cycle, spending over $76 million this quarter in various battleground Senate and House races. These include contests for Senate in Michigan, Texas and Alaska as well as House races in battlegrounds like Arizona’s 1st District and New York’s 17th District.

Wintour, Bush, Blinken among big names donating

Musk isn’t the only big name spending big in the lead up to the election.

Anna Wintour, Condé Nast’s chief content officer and global editorial director of Vogue, donated $5,000 to Talarico’s joint fundraising committee. Several members of the Soros family — Robert, Catherine and Jamison — gave a combined $15,000 to the same group.

Dallas Cowboys co-owner and chief operating officer Stephen Jones, gave $122,000 to Paxton’s joint fundraising committee, Paxton Victory, while the group received a separate $100,000 from the Dallas Cowboys’ s president and owner Jerry Jones. Major Texas GOP donor Farris Wilks gave $250,000 to his joint fundraising committee in addition to Texas businessman Alex Fairly, who gave more than $270,000. 

Four top SpaceX employees also gave more than $33,000 combined to another joint fundraising committee for Paxton, Team Paxton. 

Former President George W. Bush gave Collins $3,500 for her campaign and longtime GOP strategist Karl Rove gave her campaign $1,500. Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken gave $1,750 to Ossoff’s campaign. Seven Anthropic employees gave over $24,000 combined to Ossoff too.

Special interests hint at next moves

While some super PACs and other political groups have not yet filed — groups that report monthly will file later this month while those that file biyearly will only file again next January – the 2026 spending picture is coming into focus.

Anthropic’s political action committee spent over $250,000 between July and September, including $161,000 last month alone, according to figures first shared with The Hill. The group had a nearly even spending split between Republicans and Democrats. 

The political group gave money to both campaign arms for the Senate Republicans and Senate Democrats in addition to a handful of senators and House members on both sides.  

More recently, Think Big and American Mission, both super PACs aligned with the pro-AI Leading the Future group, have spent money in a handful of House races too.

Meanwhile, United Democracy Project, the super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, has so far spent shy of $190,000 opposing El-Sayed in the general election.  

MAHA PAC wades into Iowa governor’s race

Allies of the Make America Healthy Again (MAGA) movement are investing in the Iowa gubernatorial race to support Republican Zach Lahn. The MAHA PAC and MAHA Action PAC announced Thursday that it would be spending over $1.65 million to support Lahn as he battles against Democrat Rob Sand for the Iowa governor’s seat.  

MAHA PAC is spending $150,000 of that money on get-out-the-vote field operations while $1.5 million is being donated directly to Lahn’s campaign by MAHA Action PAC. MAHA PAC endorsed the candidate last year.  

MAHA PAC is investing in half a dozen House races, too.

Statewide races typically follow different campaign finance reporting deadlines as they vary from state to state.  

Lahn has leaned into issues aligned with the MAHA movement, particularly his focus on tackling cancer, where the Hawkeye State has one of the highest rates of new cancer.

data.title: Scaramucci on Zacharia's reported firing: 'Records are made to be broken'
data.description:
Anthony Scaramucci weighed in on Katie Zacharia’s departure as White House press secretary Friday, noting her tenure was less than his as communications director at just five days in the role.

“Records are made to be broken,” he wrote on social platform X. “But I take no pleasure in other people’s pain.”

Scaramucci famously served just 11 days as Trump’s White House communications director during the president’s first term.

Social media users have joked in recent days about whether Zacharia would last “one Scaramucci” after her first press briefing on Tuesday was heavily scrutinized. Bets were also being taken on the prediction market site Kalshi over when she would depart the role.

“The clock is running. Thus far 1/11th of a Scaramucci,” the ex-Trump official wrote online earlier this week.

A White House official confirmed to The Hill that Zacharia is “transitioning out” out of the role as the president’s top spokesperson.

She was appointed just last week to step into the role, after Karoline Leavitt left the position earlier this year. At her first briefing, Zacharia spoke for 14 minutes and took questions from only three members of the media.

Trump signaled her departure in remarks to the reporters before departing the White House for Georgia on Friday.

“I said, ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,’” the president said, referring to a conversation he said he had with Zacharia earlier. 

“I said, ‘You think about it, but I would reconsider,’” he continued. 

Zacharia had also been making headlines over her legal history. In the past she has identified herself as a lawyer on TV, but a report found that she was not licensed to practice law in any state, including California where she resides.

When asked about where she took the bar exam from reporters earlier this week, she said, “when I moved to China.”

The Wall Street Journal reported later that evening that Zacharia had failed the bar exam.

On subsequent news interviews, she failed to clear the issue up.

Zacharia told conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice that she “misheard” the question about where she took the bar exam, adding later that the test’s results were “inconsequential.”

data.title: Watch live: Trump takes campaign blitz to Georgia
data.description:
President Trump heads to Georgia Friday afternoon as Republicans look to gain ground in a closely watched Senate race with less than three weeks until the midterms.

Trump is expected to rally support for Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.), who is challenging incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). The president will also appear alongside Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson, who is facing former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D).

The visit comes after Collins and Ossoff clashed in a heated debate Tuesday over Trump’s policies, the economy and the Iran war. The Democrat has maintained a narrow lead in recent polls, adding pressure on the GOP as early voting is already underway in the Peach State.

The event in Dalton, Ga., is scheduled to begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT.

Watch live above.

data.title: Live updates: Zacharia exits White House post; Trump heads to Georgia campaign stop
data.description:
Katie Zacharia is on her way to being a former White House press secretary, after President Trump told reporters he told her to “reconsider” the position and amid a rocky start to the job this week, a White House official told The Hill.

Zacharia faced scrutiny over her legal credentials and held a short press briefing since starting the job on Monday.

Trump travels Friday to Georgia, for another stop on his red state campaigning sweep.

After visits to Alabama, Mississippi, Oklahoma, Texas, Tennessee and Kentucky over the past few weeks, he plans to make his way back to the South, where he’s slated to speak to voters Friday afternoon in Dalton, Ga.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) is joining Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed for the second day of a multicity campaigning effort throughout Michigan as he gears up to face off against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) on Election Day.

The New York lawmaker was an early supporter of El-Sayed this election season, also campaigning for him ahead of Michigan’s Democratic primary this summer.

Follow live below.

data.title: Washington Post says photographer attacked by Israeli settlers
data.description:
The Washington Post’s executive editor said Friday that Israeli settlers attacked one of its photojournalists, who was working on assignment in the West Bank.

“She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.” Matt Murray wrote in a statement shared to social platform X. “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job.”

A video capturing the incident — shared by The Post — appeared to show masked Israeli settlers attacking photographer Heidi Levine while she was on the ground, kicking her in the stomach. Separate posts by independent journalist Andrey Khrzhanovskiy, a pro-Palestinian activist, alleged the assailants also beat her with sticks.

“They took everything. They took all my stuff,” Levine said in the video when Khrzhanovskiy and other nearby journalists came to her aid. “They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times.”

After a few moments, the masked settlers began chasing Levine and the group that helped her.

Levine’s alleged assault was a part of masked settlers’ attack on a West Bank village’s annual harvest, where the attackers reportedly burned olive trees and threw rocks at Palestinians, according to Reuters — citing witnesses to the incident. The bystanders told the publication that 80 masked people carrying gas canisters had descended upon the gathering.

Palestinian medics treated Levine at a hospital in Ramallah, a city north of Jerusalem, Murray said. He added that she is now “safe.”

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu condemned the attack in a Friday morning statement, saying, “Israel unequivocally condemns violence against anyone—Jews, Arabs, Christians or journalists. Those responsible will be held accountable.”

But Netanyahu also called into question who started the encounter, as “reports indicate some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths,” he said.

The Israel prime minister added that “masked individuals on both sides [were] hurling objects,” and other recordings appear “to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual.”

“The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence,” he concluded. 

The Israeli Defense Force (IDF) and Israel Border Police similarly decried the incident and confirmed its forces had responded to it, saying, “All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means.”

“At another location where the confrontation took place, IDF soldiers initially fired warning shots into the air and then fired toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them. The confrontation was dispersed,” the IDF stated.

data.title: New dinosaur species identified from fossil tucked away in a museum
data.description:
(NewsNation) — A fossil stored in a London museum for more than a century has been identified as a new species of dinosaur.

Researchers say the new dinosaur, Invictibellatrix amberina, was identified from a skull fragment at the Natural History Museum. The fossil was first found by Reginald Walter Tooley, an amateur paleontologist, at the base of a cliff on the Isle of Wight.

After Tooley died, the museum acquired the fossil in 1924, along with more than 1,000 other specimens he had collected.

“It is a real mystery that this fossil was overlooked for so long, sitting in a drawer for nearly 100 years,” said the study’s lead author, Dr. Cassius Morrison, in a press release.

Researchers used CT scans to make 3D images of the skull and the area where the dinosaur’s brain would have been. When they compared these images to other meat-eating dinosaurs, they found some unusual features. These included an oval-shaped opening where the spinal cord met the brain and a ridge shaped like an hourglass. These differences led them to decide it was a new species.

Invictibellatrix was part of a group of meat-eating dinosaurs called megaraptorans, which were related to tyrannosaurs. It had a long, narrow head, small arms, and probably had feathers. Its claws were between 4 and 8 inches long. The dinosaur was about 10 to 13 feet long and stood around 5 feet tall, making it one of the smallest and earliest megaraptorans found so far.

Scientists believe it lived in what is now the United Kingdom about 120 million years ago. Its name means ‘unconquered female warrior,’ a reference to the group’s later role as top predators.

“It was not the apex predator of its time, but for humans this dinosaur would have been more dangerous than a T. rex,” Morrison said.

“We would have been perfectly sized prey, about a third of their body weight,” he continued. “They definitely would have chased us. A T. rex would not have bothered, as we would have been too small.”

The researchers published their findings in the journal Royal Society Open Science.
